14003-disputed-handwriting-an-exhaustive:
Jerome B. Lavay wrote Disputed Handwriting in 1909, the first American work of its kind on forgery detection. Lavay calls handwriting a gesture of the mind. He writes for banks and business houses facing check fraud. Illustrations show how experts spot altered writing.

Chapters treat chemically prepared paper, watermarks, perforating machines, and check raisers. Lavay explains how ordinary checks are raised, how perforations are filled, and how experts alter checks in reverse. His method blends science with courtroom practice. The book founded American forensic document study. It still interests students of crime and law.
15435-object-lessons-on-the-human-body-a:
This revised pupils' edition, published in New York in 1904, prints lessons given in the primary department of School No. 49 in New York City. It belongs to a series on practical work in the schoolroom, and it treats the body as the house a child lives in. Pictures support the text, and each lesson follows classroom talk between teacher and pupils.

The lessons move through the parts of the body and how to care for them, with strong warnings against alcohol and nicotine as the body's great enemies. Pupils are told to learn the sense of every word, not to repeat talk parrot-fashion, and to pay attention with their own eyes and ears. The book gives a plain view of health teaching in 1904: simple facts, moral advice, and the belief that care of the body is a daily duty.
17783-the-traveling-engineers-associatio:
The Traveling Engineers' Association issued this book of examination questions and answers for firemen seeking promotion and new men seeking employment, to improve the locomotive engine service of American railroads. Copyright belonged to W. O. Thompson in March 1911, with a revision in January 1919. Its preface states the railroads' policy plainly.

Railroads employed firemen who would in time become competent locomotive engineers, which required at least a common school education, good habits, good physical condition, and alertness. Readers get a working exam manual for the footplate, practical and demanding. The book suits railway historians and readers of working life.
18274-a-book-of-natural-history-young-fo:
Volume fourteen of the Young Folks' Library gathers natural history selections for young readers, published at Boston by Hall and Locke. The series promised selections from the choicest literature of all lands, in twenty richly illustrated volumes, covering folk lore, fairy tales, wonders of earth, sea, and sky, animal stories, and biography. This volume turns that promise to the living world.

Its contents pair famous writers with plain subjects: David Starr Jordan on animals, birds, and fishes, T. H. Huxley on the wonder of life and the man-like apes, Margaret Warner Morley on frogs, Grant Allen on strange nurseries, and John Burroughs on birds' nests. Darwin writes on the scissor beak and the condor. Young readers get natural history as good reading: short pieces by masters, with pictures to match.
19109-poems-vol-iv:
Hattie Howard wrote this fourth volume of poems, published in Hartford in 1904. Press notices praise her verse as natural, direct, and sunny, with a laugh at the end of many fanciful pieces. The book gathers sentiment, humour, and moral reflection in a wholesome, human spirit.

An apple tree poem praises the farmer who digs, grafts, and stores fruit for winter, learning thrift from squirrels, while other verses muse on old tales of husbands, wives, and Satan's wiles. Readers get cheerful, old-style American verse, modest in aim and warm in tone.
20204-the-storm-cloud-of-the-nineteenth-:
John Ruskin gave The Storm-Cloud of the Nineteenth Century as two lectures in 1884. The first lecture is printed much as he gave it on February 4. He repeated it on February 11 with several passages enlarged. Its last part changed to suit a wider public interest then.

Ruskin saw a new, dark haze fouling skies he had known as bright. He blamed coal smoke and industry for that grim storm-cloud. The lectures mix sharp sky watching with moral anger at pollution. Readers get an early, vivid warning on air and industry from a master critic.
20956-in-the-yule-log-glow-book-iv:
God rest you merry, gentlemen, rings out in In the Yule-Log Glow, Book Four, from 1891. The carol's tidings of comfort and joy set the volume's Christmas key. Harrison Weir and others gathered tales to match that glow of hearth and hymn.

Stories, poems, and carols for the season fill book four of this holiday set. Snow, bells, feasts, and kindly deeds warm its pages in turn. Victorian Christmas books fed a new cult of the festive home. This one shows the trade at its coziest, made to be read aloud while the yule log burned low.
21671-army-boys-on-the-firing-line-or-ho:
Homer Randall sends his Army Boys against the German drive in Army Boys on the Firing Line, copyrighted in 1919. Frank and Tom Bradford trade fire with raiders who rush their line. The last rush, Tom jokes, went back in a bigger hurry than it came.

Front pictures show Frank hurling his revolver in a sentry's face. Chapters promise capture, a midnight swim, a drugged detachment, and a mined bridge. Nick Rabig turns up again as the tale's villain. Randall's series, begun with Army Boys in France, gave American boys a brisk, patriotic tale of the Great War's last year.
21775-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
British and Irish prose from 1672 to 1800 fills this fourth volume of The Best of the World's Classics, published in 1909. Henry Cabot Lodge served as editor-in-chief, with Francis W. Halsey beside him. The volume is the second of two covering Great Britain and Ireland. Portraits of Johnson, Goldsmith, Pope, and Gibbon front the book.

Inside, readers meet Sir Richard Steele in pieces from The Guardian, The Spectator, and The Tatler, including Sir Roger and the Widow. Lord Bolingbroke follows, writing on the shortness of life and the study of history. Each author comes with a short life and notes. The set aimed to put the world's best prose, briefly framed, into ordinary homes.
22254-the-substance-of-a-journal-during-:
John West, a Church of England chaplain, kept a journal at the Red River Colony in the years 1820 to 1823. West was the Hudson's Bay Company's first Protestant chaplain in the Northwest. His Substance of a Journal appeared as missionary interest in British North America was rising. He writes of a day when distant parts of the earth were opening to missionary labour, and British sympathy with them.

West describes Lord Selkirk's settlers, the fur trade, Indigenous peoples, and brutal winters. He founded a school and a church on the Red River, in what is now Manitoba. The journal is a founding document of western Canada.
22343-the-wedding-ring-a-series-of-disco:
T. De Witt Talmage preached The Wedding Ring, a series of discourses for husbands and wives, in 1896. Talmage was a famous American preacher of his day. His talks take marriage cases straight from Scripture.

One discourse opens with Samson, the giant of the Bible. Samson asks his parents to consent to a marriage they judge unfit. He was wise, Talmage says, to ask their counsel. He was not wise in rejecting it once given. From such stories the sermons draw rules for home life. Readers get Victorian marriage teaching in a preacher's strong, plain, and confident voice.
23317-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
John Richard Green wrote this fourth volume of his History of the English People, covering the Reformation from fifteen forty to fifteen ninety-three, in a London edition of the late eighteen hundreds. Book six opens with the Protestant revolution, then the Catholic reaction under Mary.

Later chapters turn to the England of Elizabeth, her early reign, and the shaping of a Protestant nation. Green's history, beloved for its vivid narrative, made the past live for general readers, and this volume covers its most fateful religious turn. One writer calls keeping the oath of allegiance plain rebellion against God, and names a Jezebel of England.
23472-a-history-of-the-four-georges-and-:
Justin McCarthy, with Justin Huntly McCarthy, closed this history with a fourth volume covering the later Georges and William the Fourth, printed in nineteen hundred one. The set's master index lives in this volume, and its year and subject side notes help readers track courts, ministries, and events across a long, changing age.

From Regency glitter to reform, railways, and a new king's short reign, the volume follows Britain as it moves toward modern party politics and wider votes. McCarthy writes with narrative ease, pairing state affairs with social scenes and sharp portraits. Readers who reach this final volume will find the story brought to a fitting close, with the index making the whole set easy to use for study or for browsing.
6154-athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-iv:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's fourth book runs from the end of the Persian invasion to Cimon's death, 479 to 449 BC. It treats war's effects, Sparta's interference with Athens's fortifications, Themistocles's dexterous conduct, the new harbor of Piraeus, and the allied fleet at Cyprus and Byzantium.

Pausanias changes character, turns ambitious and treasonous, and is recalled, while Athens rises to head the Ionian League, Delos becomes senate and treasury, and Aristides manages ably. Cimon takes fleet command, Eion falls, Scyros is colonized, and Themistocles is ostracized. This book alone is described here. Aristides and Cimon guide Athens through war and league politics.
7563-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-l:
The Duchesse d'Orleans, sister-in-law of Louis XIV, wrote letters and memoirs full of court gossip, and this volume gathers short passages and pictures from them. A German princess at Versailles, she kept a frank, outsider's eye on French manners. Each passage can be traced to its full scene, so her sharpest remarks keep their context. The pictures add faces to the names she discusses.

Read together, the passages sketch Versailles as one plain-spoken witness saw it. Manners, dress, duplicity, and the gap between show and truth recur across them. She is funny about fashions and blunt about conduct, and she spares neither queens nor courtiers. It is a lively way into the Sun King's court: gossip with a point, from a woman who never quite belonged to it.
7565-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-l:
The Duc de Saint-Simon, the great memorialist of Louis XIV's court, is the source of this volume of short passages and pictures. It is distinct from the Duchesse d'Orleans volume of the same title, which gives a different witness to the same reign. Saint-Simon watched Versailles for years and judged its people without mercy. Each passage can be traced to its full scene.

Read together, the passages sketch a court built on rank, favor, and close watching. Kingship, friendship, pride, and the cost of plain speech recur across them. Saint-Simon insists that a king exists for his subjects, not the reverse, and he distrusts flattery and invention. It is Versailles as a proud, observant insider saw it: brilliant on the surface, unforgiving underneath.
7966-the-child-and-childhood-in-folk-tho:
Alexander Francis Chamberlain, M. A. , Ph. D. , expanded his 1894 Clark University lectures into this study of the child in folk thought. He examines what children do and mean among so-called primitive peoples, then traces analogues and survivals of those ideas in modern civilisation. The book ranges across custom, play, belief, and language, treating childhood as a subject for science as much as for sentiment.

Chamberlain writes for teachers and students of the new child-study movement, but his examples keep the book lively. Readers learn how widely cultures have marked, protected, and imagined children, and how much of that old lore still lives in nursery custom. It is a pioneering work of anthropology, and still a rich source for the history of childhood.
8070-expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-jo:
Alexander Maclaren's expositions on the Gospel of John, chapters one to fourteen, work through the Gospel sermon by sermon. His titles trace the book's opening movement: The Word in Eternity, in the World, and in the Flesh; The Light and the Lamps. The Fulness of Christ; Grace and Truth; The World's Sin-Bearer; and studies of the first disciples, John and Andrew, Simon Peter, Philip, and Nathanael. Later expositions cover the first miracle and Jesus the joy-bringer.

Maclaren preaches John as a Gospel of light and life, drawing each passage toward personal faith. His commentary suits readers who want to linger over John's discourses rather than rush through them. The volume is a solid companion for devotional study of the fourth Gospel's first half.
9584-the-tent-on-the-beach-and-other-poe:
Part four of volume four of Whittier's works centers on The Tent on the Beach, a poem of a seaside picnic in verse. Whittier pitches his tent near Hampton's salt meadows, with friends Fields and Taylor as his companions. The part also holds The Wreck of Rivermouth, The Grave by the Lake, and The Brother of Mercy. The Changeling, The Maids of Attitash, and Kallundborg Church follow.

Later poems include The Cable Hymn, The Dead Ship of Harpswell, and Abraham Davenport, each a tale of sea, faith, or fate. Whittier writes with ease and warmth, as if swapping stories by firelight. A reader gets a beachside storybook in verse, rich in New England coast lore and gentle moral light.
9759-leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-:
Book four of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila, or The Siege of Granada, opens with Leila in the castle as the siege breaks anew. Boabdil el Chico takes the field with a numerous army, striking fortress after fortress left by Ferdinand. Terror spreads as mountain tribes pour down from the Sierra Nevada snows. Each day swells Boabdil's ranks with fresh recruits.

Leila's holy anxieties yield to the fearful news that grips every castle dweller. A fugitive and a meeting, named in later chapters, deepen the tale. A reader gets the fourth book of a Granada romance, where a Moorish king's last campaign shakes the siege.
992-a-theological-political-treatise-par:
In this closing part of his treatise, Baruch Spinoza turns from how to read scripture to how faith should stand beside civil rule. He argues that true religion asks for justice and charity, not for creeds enforced by law, and that a free state harms no pious mind. The Dutch thinker wrote when churches and rulers still policed belief.

Spinoza holds that rulers should guard peace and safety, while minds stay free to judge and speak. Faith kept simple, he says, binds people in love rather than in strife. The argument ends his case for tolerance, and it has shaped later thought on church, state, and the rights of conscience.
a-theological-political-treatise-part-iv:
Baruch Spinoza closes his Theologico-Political Treatise with part four, chapters sixteen to twenty, on the state and the rights of rulers and subjects. He begins with nature, where right reaches as far as power does. From there he asks how people pass from that rough state into civil order.

The chapters define civil right and wrong, treaties, and treason, then test his ideas against the old Hebrew republic under Moses and after. Spinoza argues that no one can give up all his rights to a ruler, and that a state stays safest when people may think and speak freely. The part ends his case for free thought.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-iv:
In 1865 Barbier de Meynard issued the fourth tome of Les Prairies d'Or, his French version of the Muruj al-Dhahab. Al-Masudi composed the Meadows of Gold in the tenth century after years of travel through the Islamic world and beyond. The Société Asiatique set runs to nine tomes in all.

Across the work, history and geography walk hand in hand. The lands of the earth come with their kings, faiths, customs, and marvels. Then the annals of Islam run down to the author's lifetime. Al-Masudi quotes poets, sailors, and court scholars with equal delight. Meynard's French, aided by Pavet de Courteille, became the standard Masudi for Europe. Tome four keeps the long narrative moving.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-iv:
Book IV of Athens: Its Rise and Fall, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, runs from the Persian invasion's end to the death of Cimon. Its heading dates the span 479 to 449 BC. Lytton opens with remarks on the effects of war and praise for the French philosophers who first stripped war of its delusive glory. Then Themistocles outwits Sparta over Athens' new walls and builds the harbor of the Piraeus, while Pausanias, the Spartan victor of Plataea, rots into ambition and treason abroad.

The Ionians revolt from Spartan command, Athens rises to head their league, and Delos becomes the allies' senate and treasury under the prudent management of Aristides. Cimon succeeds to the fleet, colonizes Scyros, and brings home the supposed bones of Theseus. Themistocles falls and is ostracized, Aristides dies, and the constitution bends further toward democracy. Empire is assembled piece by piece. Each piece is defensible. The sum is transformative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-iv:
Boniface IV, pope from 608 to 615, turned Rome's Pantheon into the first pagan temple remade as a Christian church. Son of a Marsian physician named John, he served Gregory the Great as deacon and steward of the papal estates. Consecrated on 25 August 608 after a vacancy of nine months, he gained Phocas's leave to consecrate the Pantheon to Mary and all martyrs on 13 May 609.

Twenty-eight cartloads of bones were moved from the catacombs to a porphyry basin beneath the high altar. Mellitus, first Bishop of London, visited Rome to consult him on the young English Church and carried home a council decree and papal letters. Columban of Bobbio later wrote sharply, charging him with heresy over the Three Chapters, yet their relations seem untroubled. He died in May 615.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clement-xiv:
Clement the Fourteenth, born Lorenzo Ganganelli at Sant'Arcangelo near Rimini on 31 October 1705 and dead at Rome on 22 September 1774, inherited a Church in dire distress. Gallicanism, Jansenism, Febronianism, and Rationalism rose against papal authority. The rulers of France, Spain, Naples, Portugal, and Parma sided with the sectarians. 

The great question was suppressing the Society of Jesus. Suppression had already taken place in fact in France, Spain, and Portugal. The new pope's accession became the occasion for demanding abolition root and branch, in law as well as fact, worldwide. The conclave of 15 February 1769 suffered rare interference and intrigue. French and Spanish ambassadors with Cardinals de Bernis and Orsini pressed the campaign. The forty-seven cardinals split between Court cardinals and Zelanti, with the Jesuit-favourable latter holding the majority. Bernis refused to make election depend on a written engagement to suppress the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-iv:
Henry IV, king of France and Navarre, was born at Pau in 1553 to Jeanne d'Albret and Antoine de Bourbon and led the Protestant party in the wars of religion from 1569. As heir-presumptive from 1584 he faced Sixtus V's declaration that he had forfeited throne and Navarre. On Henry III's death in 1589 he took the crown with Protestants, politiques, and many Catholics behind him. 

From March 1592 the convert Jacques Davy du Perron shaped Henry's thinking. After conferences at Mantes the king questioned bishops for five hours on saints, confession, and papal authority, signed a formula of adhesion, and made his abjuration at Saint-Denis on 25 July 1593. The famous line Paris is well worth a Mass, the entry notes, appears in no contemporary document. Regularization by Rome, which had excommunicated him, still remained. His reign ran until his assassination in 1610.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-xiv:
Louis XIV, the Sun King, ruled France from 1643 to 1715, born at Saint-Germain in 1638 and dead at Versailles. Son of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, he took the throne as a child, with Cardinal Mazarin ruling until 1661 and winning Alsace, Artois, and Roussillon for France.

Taking personal rule in 1661, Louis bent nobles into courtiers and tamed the parlements. He gathered all power through intendants and ministers: Colbert for finance, Louvois for war, and Lionne for foreign affairs. This huge survey follows his wars, his building, his revocation of the Edict of Nantes, and his long twilight, when glory curdled into debt and defeat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nerses-i-iv:
Nerses is the name of several Armenian patriarchs, treated together in this entry. Nerses I, surnamed the Great, died in 373. Born of royal stock, he spent his youth in Caesarea, married Sanducht, a Mamikonian princess, and after her death became chamberlain to King Arshak. Entering the ecclesiastical state, he was elected catholicos in 353.

His patriarchate opened a new era, bringing the Church closer to the people after its identification with royalty and nobles. At Ashtishat he issued laws on marriage, fast days and worship, built schools and hospitals, and sent monks to preach across the land. Reforms angered the king, who exiled him, probably to Edessa. Recalled under King Bab in 369, he barred the dissolute ruler from church, and Bab, feigning reconciliation, poisoned him at table. Later Nerses patriarchs, builders and scholars, complete the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-iv:
Otto IV, German king and Roman emperor, was born near Argentan about 1182 and died on 19 May 1218, son of Henry the Lion and Mathilda, daughter of Henry II of England. Backed by his uncle Richard the Lion-Heart, he won Guelph and English support. After Henry VI died and the Hohenstaufens chose Philip of Swabia, Adolf of Cologne proclaimed Otto king at Cologne on 9 June 1198.

Pope Innocent III, hostile to the Hohenstaufens, at first waited, keen above all to hold the right to judge disputed German elections. After Philip seized Mainz against canon law, Innocent declared for Otto in 1201. Philip's murder at Bamberg in 1208 rallied the princes to Otto, but his cause broke at Bouvines on 27 July 1214, when Philip Augustus crushed the Guelph and English host. Absolved from excommunication, Otto died after failed bids in 1217 and 1218.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-i:
Pope Adrian IV, an English-born pope elected in December 1154, was born about 1100 and died on 1 September 1159. Little certain is known of his boyhood, and the reliable accounts come from Cardinal Boso and John of Salisbury. Boso says Adrian was born in or near Saint Albans, left England young to study, and took vows as an Austin canon near Avignon.

Elected abbot, he was kept at Rome by Eugenius III and made cardinal and Bishop of Albano in 1146. Matthew Paris adds that the abbot of Saint Albans first turned the young man away as unready for monastic life. It is now thought fairly certain he was born at Abbot's Langley in Hertfordshire about 1100. His father was Robert Brekespear, a man of humble means, and he went abroad as a poor wandering scholar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-alexande:
Pope Alexander IV reigned from 1254 to 1261, born Rinaldo Conti of the house of Segni, which had already given the papacy Innocent III and Gregory IX. Made cardinal-deacon in 1227 by his uncle Gregory IX and cardinal-bishop of Ostia four years later, he inherited Gregory's care for the Franciscan Order. On Innocent IV's death at Naples in December 1254 the aged cardinal was unanimously chosen, protesting, the entry says, that he yielded only reluctantly.

Matthew of Paris paints him as kind, religious, assiduous in prayer, and strict in abstinence, but easily swayed by flatterers and avaricious advisers. Those advisers pushed him to continue Innocent's war of extermination against Frederick II's heirs, the infant Conradin and the formidable Manfred in Apulia. In March 1255 he excommunicated Manfred and granted the kingdom of the Two Sicilies to Edmund of Lancaster, Henry III's second son.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-anastasi:
Pope Anastasius IV was crowned on 12 July 1153 and died at Rome on 3 December of the following year. His short pontificate is chiefly remembered for two acts: the restoration of the Pantheon, achieved through his exertions, and special privileges granted to the Hospitallers of Saint John of Jerusalem.

He is best known for his stance toward Frederick Barbarossa and his recognition of Wichmann as Bishop of Magdeburg, by which he ended an ecclesiastical quarrel. His surviving works consist of some letters and a treatise on the Trinity, a modest literary legacy for a pope whose reign lasted barely seventeen months.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict IV, a Roman and son of Mammalus, became pope in the first half of 900 and died in the summer of 903. His reign falls in the darkest period of papal history, when many reigns were short and little is known of their deeds. The contemporary historian Frodoard loudly praised his high birth, generosity, and zeal for the public good, giving him the title Great.

His chief historic act was crowning Louis the Blind as emperor. He upheld Formosus's decision for Argrim's claim to Langres, supported Stephen, Bishop of Naples, and excommunicated the assassin of Fulk, Archbishop of Reims. He offered practical sympathy to Malacenus, Bishop of Amasia, driven from his see by Saracen advances. He granted privileges to Fulda and other monasteries. He was buried before Saint Peter's near the gate of Guido.

Pope Benedict XIV, born Prospero Lorenzo Lambertini at Bologna on 31 March 1675, was perhaps the greatest scholar among the popes. Schooled by tutors and at the Collegium Clementianum in Rome, he took doctorates in theology and in canon and civil law at nineteen in 1694. His favourite author was Saint Thomas Aquinas, but his bent ran to history and law.

He rose through the Curia as consistorial advocate and consultor of the Holy Office. He became Promotor of the Faith in 1708, bishop of Ancona in 1727, cardinal in 1728, and archbishop of Bologna in 1731. Enormous application and more than ordinary cleverness made him one of the most erudite men of his time. His devotion to science, history, and letters, including Tasso, Dante, and Ariosto, gave energy to his thought and life to his style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-celestin: Pope Celestine IV, born Gofredo Castiglioni of Milan, nephew of Urban III and probably a Cistercian, died on 10 November 1241. Gregory IX made him cardinal, and he succeeded Gregory on 25 October 1241 at the height of the papal war with Emperor Frederick II. He died after a reign of fifteen days. His sources include Labbe and Cossart's collection of councils and Argelati's Milanese library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement IV, born Guido Le Gros at Saint-Gilles on the Rhone on 23 November, year unknown, was elected at Perugia on 5 February 1265. He died at Viterbo on 29 November 1268. After Urban IV's death on 2 October 1264, the cardinals at Perugia debated four months. They weighed continuing war against the Hohenstaufen by calling in Charles of Anjou against finding another way to secure papal independence.

No other solution offering itself, they united on the Cardinal-Bishop of Sabina, a Frenchman and subject of Charles. Guido was of noble extraction. His father, the knight Foulquois, entered a Carthusian monastery after his mother's death. Guido married, served briefly as a soldier, then studied law under Durandus and gained a national reputation as an advocate. Saint Louis made him a trusted councillor. Widowed with two daughters, he took Holy orders, becoming Bishop of Puy in 1256, Archbishop of Narbonne in 1259, and cardinal in December 1261.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-eugene-i:
Pope Eugene IV, born Gabriello Condulmaro at Venice in 1383, was elected on 4 March 1431 and died at Rome on 23 February 1447. Nephew of Gregory XII on his mother's side, he gave 20,000 ducats to the poor. He entered the Augustinian monastery of Saint George and at twenty-four became Bishop of Siena, resigning when Siena objected to a foreign ruler. In 1408 he became Cardinal-Priest of Saint Clement.

He served Martin V as legate in the March of Ancona, quelling a Bolognese sedition, and the conclave elected him on the first scrutiny. He kept his monastic routine and regularity on the throne. Hatred of nepotism plunged him into a fierce war with the Colonna, settled only when Florence, Venice, and Naples aided him and the Colonna paid 75,000 ducats. Scarcely was that danger past when the Council of Basle, convoked by Martin V, opened the struggle that troubled his whole reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-felix-iv:
Pope Felix IV reigned from 526 to 530, chosen at the Gothic king's wish after John I died in prison at Ravenna on 18 May 526, a victim of Theodoric's suspicions. Through Theodoric's influence the cardinal-priest Felix of Samnium, son of Castorius, was brought forward, and clergy and laity yielded to the Arian king's wish. He was consecrated Bishop of Rome on 12 July 526 and used Theodoric's favour well.

After Theodoric's death on 30 August 526, Amalasuntha, ruling for Athalaric, answered the clergy's complaint against civil usurpation with an edict. Drafted by Cassiodorus, it confirmed that charges by laymen against clerics go to the pope or his court, under a fine of ten pounds of gold for violators. She gave him the Temple of Romulus and the land-registry office in the Forum. He turned them into Saints Cosmas and Damian and sent capitula on grace and free will that Orange adopted in 529.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory IV was elected near the end of 827 and died in January 844. A Roman and son of John, he had been Cardinal-Priest of Saint Mark's, which he adorned with mosaics. Paschal I ordained him priest for his piety and learning. Raised to Peter's chair despite protests of unfitness, he could not be consecrated until Louis the Pious approved his election. That delayed his government until March 828.

Most of his reign was spent in Louis's quarrels with his sons. Louis's deed of 817 had divided the empire among Lothair, Pepin, and Louis the German. His second wife Judith pushed the interests of their son Charles the Bald. The elder brothers seized and imprisoned their father in 830, then quarrelled, and Louis was restored at Nijmegen. Louis's favour to Charles drove his sons to arms again, and Lothair induced Gregory to cross the Alps, making the pope seem the rebels' ally.

Pope Gregory XIV, born Niccolò Sfondrati at Somma near Milan on 11 February 1535, was elected on 5 December 1590 and died at Rome on 15 October 1591. His father Francesco, a Milanese senator, became cardinal after his wife's death in 1544. Niccolò studied at Perugia and Padua, was ordained priest, became Bishop of Cremona in 1560, sat at Trent from 1561 to 1563, and was made cardinal by Gregory XIII in December 1583.

Urban VII died on 27 September 1590, and after a conclave of more than two months Sfondrati was chosen, though he had not sought the tiara. Found kneeling before a crucifix, he wept on election and cried, God forgive you, what have you done. A man of piety and mortification, friend of Charles Borromeo and Philip Neri, he threw his energy behind the French League against Henry of Navarre. Sixtus V had declared Henry heretic and barred him from the French throne, and Spain encouraged the League.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-honorius:
Pope Honorius IV, born Giacomo Savelli at Rome about 1210, was elected on 2 April 1285 and died at Rome on 3 April 1287. Of the rich Savelli and grandnephew of Honorius III, he studied at Paris, held a prebend at Châlons, and became Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin in 1261. Martin IV made him papal prefect in Tuscany and captain of the army, and with three cardinals he invested Charles of Anjou as ruler of Sicily in 1265.

He was one of six cardinals who elected Gregory X by compromise at Viterbo in 1271, attended Lyons in 1274, and negotiated with Rudolf of Habsburg for Adrian V in 1276. After Martin IV died at Perugia on 28 March 1285, fifteen cardinals met. Skipping Gregory X's conclave rules as suspended by John XXI, they elected Savelli at the vote. It was one of the fastest elections in papal history, driven by Sicilian urgency and fear of Angevin interference.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent IV, born Sinibaldo de' Fieschi, Count of Lavagna, at Genoa, was elected on 25 June 1243 and died at Naples on 7 December 1254. Educated at Parma and Bologna, he taught canon law at Bologna. He became canon at Parma, auditor of the Curia in 1226, cardinal-priest in 1227, vice-chancellor in 1228, and Bishop of Albenga and legate in northern Italy in 1235.

When Celestine IV died after sixteen days, Frederick II, holding the Papal States around Rome, tried to intimidate the cardinals into a compliant choice. They fled to Anagni and chose Fieschi after an interregnum of nineteen months. Once Frederick's friend, Innocent knew from Gregory IX's experience how little imperial promises were worth. He refused the emperor's messengers as excommunicate, then sent legates to Melfi. They demanded restoration of the Papal States, release of captive prelates, and amends, with a council of kings and prelates to judge if Frederick denied wrongdoing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-iv:
Pope John IV, a native of Dalmatia and son of the scholasticus Venantius, reigned from 640 to 642 and died on 12 October 642. He was the Roman Church's archdeacon when elected. His consecration came hard on his election, a sign that Ravenna's resident exarchs now confirmed papal elections. Slav invasions were troubling his homeland, and drew his attention there.

To relieve the inhabitants, John dispatched Abbot Martin to Dalmatia and Istria carrying large sums for ransoming captives. As ruined churches could not be rebuilt, Rome received relics of great Dalmatian saints. John built an oratory to honour them, adorned with mosaics showing John holding a model of his oratory. He also endeavoured to convert the Slavs. While still pope-elect, he joined the Roman Church's other rulers in condemning Monothelism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xiv:
Pope John XIV, birth date unknown, died in 984. Benedict VII's death left Bishop Peter Campanora of Pavia, once Italy's imperial chancellor, chosen pope with Otto II's blessing. Coronation came late in November or early in December 983, and he took John's name. That same year, on 7 December, young Otto II died at Rome, with the pope readying him for death, and found burial in Saint Peter's vestibule.

Boniface VII, antipope since 974 through Crescentius's Roman partisans, learned of the emperor's death at Constantinople and hurried back to Rome in April 984. His partisans helped him seize John, lock him in Castel Sant'Angelo, and take the throne. Four months on, the wretched John XIV perished in prison 20 August 984, starved and broken, or else murdered at Boniface's command.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-martin-i:
Simon de Brie was born at Montpensier in Touraine. He served as treasurer at St Martin in Tours. He became chancellor of France under Louis IX. He was made cardinal in 1262. His legations in France included offering Sicily to Charles of Anjou. After Nicholas III died, Charles pressed hard at Viterbo. He had two Italian cardinals jailed. That pressure helped secure Simon's unanimous election in February 1281.

Simon was crowned at Orvieto. A French pope was hated at Rome. Martin leaned wholly on Charles. He broke the 1274 union with the Greek church. He did so by excommunicating Emperor Michael Palaeologus. He spent his full power trying to hold Sicily for France after the Sicilian Vespers. All of it failed. He died at Perugia in March 1285.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-nicholas:
Girolamo Masci was born at Ascoli to a humble family. He joined the Franciscans young. He was sent to Constantinople to invite the Greeks to the Second Council of Lyons. He succeeded St Bonaventure as head of his order. He was made cardinal in 1278. He became bishop of Palestrina in 1281. He was unanimously elected pope in February 1288. A conclave thinned by fever had chosen him.

He was the first Franciscan pope. He took his name in memory of Nicholas III. He ruled under heavy Colonna influence at Rome. That sway was so open that wits pictured him cased in a column. Only his tiara showed above it. Rudolf of Habsburg's bid for the imperial crown from his hands failed. The entry follows his reign to his death at Rome in April 1292.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-iv:
Giovanni Pietro Caraffa was born near Benevento in 1476. The Caraffa were a great noble house of Naples. Cardinal Oliviero Caraffa guided his young kinsman's training. He brought him to the papal court in 1494. He gave up the see of Chieti in his favour. From that Latin name, Theate, Giovanni Pietro took the tag Theatinus.

Leo X sent him to England and Spain, where life sharpened his hatred of Spanish rule at home. In 1524 he gave up his benefices and joined St Cajetan's clerics regular, the Theatines, as their first general. Elected pope in 1555 against the emperor's wishes, he held high the banner of Italian independence for four years. He had rebuilt the Inquisition in Italy on papal lines. The entry paints an austere patriot, and ends with his death in August 1559.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-iv:
Giovanni Angelo Medici was born at Milan in 1499. His father farmed taxes. His elder brother Giangiacomo became a soldier of fortune, Marquis of Marignano, and conqueror of Siena. Giovanni studied philosophy, medicine, and law at Pavia and Bologna, taking a doctorate in law. He reached Rome on 26 December 1527, exactly thirty-two years before his election.

Paul III trusted him and used him to govern papal cities, and made him cardinal late in his reign. As pope, Pius IV first granted amnesty to those who had insulted Paul IV's memory. He tried and executed Paul's kinsmen Carlo Caraffa and his brother, a sentence later judged unjust. He freed Cardinal Morone and others jailed on suspicion of heresy. He then gave himself to finishing the Council of Trent, with his cardinal-nephew St Charles Borromeo at his side. He died at Rome in December 1565.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-le:
Leo IV, a Roman, son of Radoald, won unanimous election as Sergius II's successor. After the Saracen raid on Rome in 846, fear for the city led to his consecration on 10 April 847 without the emperor's consent. At once he set about guarding Rome against another raid.

He repaired the walls and rebuilt fifteen great towers. He was the first to wall the Vatican hill, with imperial money and help from Roman cities and colonies. Four years' work produced the Leonine City, blessed with great solemnity in 852. Meanwhile a Saracen fleet sailing for Rome was destroyed off Ostia in 849 by allied fleets and a tempest. He rebuilt Portus for Corsican exiles driven out by Saracen raids. In 850 he crowned Lothair's son Louis as fellow emperor, and in 853 he anointed the child Alfred as king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sergius-:
Sergius IV was born Peter Pig's Snout, son of Peter the Shoemaker of Rome's ninth region. Before taking the name Sergius he was bishop of Albano from 1004 to 1009. He was consecrated about 31 July 1009. He checked John Crescentius, the Patricius who dominated Rome, by strengthening the party favouring the Germans.

Little is known of his doings beyond grants of privilege. Papyrus originals of some survive. By them he freed several monasteries from episcopal jurisdiction. Though his temporal power was small, nobles placed lands under his protection. He proved a great friend of the poor in famine. He died on 12 May 1012 and was buried in the Lateran Basilica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sixtus-i:
Francesco della Rovere was born near Abisola in 1414 to poor parents. As a child he was destined for the Franciscans. He studied philosophy and theology at Pavia and lectured at Padua, Bologna, Pavia, Siena, and Florence. His pupils included Cardinal Bessarion. Paul II made him cardinal of San Pietro in Vincoli in 1467. In 1470 he issued a study of the Precious Blood and a study of the Immaculate Conception.

Elected on Paul II's death, his first thought was war against the Turks. Legates went to France, Spain, Germany, Hungary, and Poland, but the crusade brought back only twenty-five prisoners paraded through Rome. He then turned to Italian politics and heaped riches on unworthy relations. His nephew Cardinal Riario plotted the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478 to topple the Medici. Sixtus knew of the plot, put Florence under interdict, and fought a two-year war with the city. He died on 12 August 1484.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-:
Stephen, a Sicilian and son of Olivus, was born about 720 and died on 1 or 3 August 772. Trouble over Paul I's successor began before Paul died: Toto of Nepi burst into Rome with Tuscans and forced his layman brother Constantine into Peter's chair in June 767. In spring 768 Christopher and his son Sergius escaped, and with Lombard help deposed the usurper and the monk Philip.

By their efforts Stephen, a Benedictine monk ordained priest by Zachary, was canonically elected and consecrated on 7 August 768. Afterward the antipopes were treated with great cruelty Stephen apparently could not prevent. To bar repeats, the Lateran council of April 769 forbade laymen as popes or electors: only cardinals should be chosen. Stephen backed Leo of Ravenna against a lay intruder, and with Charlemagne and Carloman's support recovered lands from the Lombards. Desiderius struck back, marrying his daughter to Charlemagne and engineering the fall of Christopher and Sergius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-iv:
Jacques Pantaléon, later Urban IV, reigned from 1261 to 1264. A French cobbler's son, born at Troyes, he died at Perugia on 2 October 1264. He rose from canon of Laon to archdeacon of Liège, catching Innocent IV's eye at Lyons in 1245. In 1247 he went to Germany, working in Silesia. Verdun's bishopric came to him in 1253, Jerusalem's patriarchate in 1255.

On Alexander IV's death in May 1261, Pantaléon was at Viterbo. After a three-month conclave, he was elected on 29 August 1261. He inherited Alexander's two heavy tasks: Sicily and Rome's lost Italian influence. He set aside a crusade to restore the fallen Latin Empire; home tasks came first. At Rome he won recognition of his sovereignty without ever risking a visit. By mid-1263 he had restored order in the Papal States, weakened Manfred's Lombard alliances, and revived Tuscany's crushed Guelphs. Sicily still needed a foreign conqueror.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-iv:
Raymond the Fourth, Count of Toulouse and of Tripoli, was born about 1043 and died at Tripoli in 1105. This encyclopedia entry names him son of Raymond the Third, Pons, and notes that in 1088 he succeeded his brother William the Fourth, who died without male issue. From 1066 he had held Rouergue, Nîmes and Narbonne, making him one of the powerful lords of southern France. In 1095 he welcomed Pope Urban the Second on his own estates and took the Cross.

He vowed to stay away from his own dominions for good. Following a pilgrimage to Chaise Dieu, he departed in October 1096, leaving his lands to Bertrand. His army of Aquitanians and Provençals marched with the legate Adhémar of Monteil. They crossed Lombardy to Constantinople through the Eastern Alps, fighting successful combats with the Slavs of that region. Vaissette, Chalandon and Bréhier supply the entry's crusade sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-canute-iv:
St. Canute IV, also spelled Cnut, was martyr and king of Denmark, date of birth uncertain. He died on 10 July 1086, the third of Sweyn II Estridsen's thirteen natural sons. This entry follows a man elected king on his brother Harold's death about 1080. He warred on his barbarous enemies and brought Courland and Livonia to the faith. He married Eltha, daughter of Robert, count of Flanders, and had a son Charles, surnamed the Good.

He was a strong ruler, as his stern dealing with the pirate Eigill of Bornholm proves. His people's happiness and the Church's interests were the objects he had most at heart. To Roskilde cathedral, still the royal burying place, he gave his own diadem. His austerity matched his assiduity in prayer. An expedition to England for the Saxons against William the Conqueror, planned in 1085, failed through his brother Olaf's treachery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-iv:
Victor IV is the name of two antipopes, rival claimants to the papacy in the twelfth century. The first, Cardinal Gregory Conti, was elected in March 1138 by Pierleoni partisans as successor to Anacletus II against Innocent II. Submitted to Innocent and renounced office after only two months, on 29 May.

The second, Octavian, Cardinal of St Cecilia, was elected in September 1159 by a small minority of cardinals, St Peter's clergy. The Roman populace, while the majority chose Chancellor Rolando as Alexander III. Octavian, of the powerful Tusculan counts, popular for liberality and splendid living and friendly to the Germans, rested his hopes on Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. The emperor, at first neutral, convoked a synod at Pavia in 1160 that decided for Victor and anathematized Alexander, deepening the schism until Victor's death at Lucca in 1164.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pre-Assassinati: Maxwell Lehman, civil service leader, is the subject named in this pre-assassination-era declassified US government file. The Internet Archive's record offers the title alone - no date, no context. No public text found. A name from the files, kept on record.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-iv:
Book Four of Lytton's Leila opens inside a besieged castle. News breaks in on Leila's calm prayers and holy anxieties. Every inhabitant of the castle feels the fearful interest of that news.

The siege of Granada now touches daily life directly. Moors and Christians prepare for the struggle's hardest phase. Leila's love and faith face their sharpest tests yet. Lytton slows the war to show one woman's inner battle. The fourth book readies readers for the great battle ahead. Almamen the enchanter gives the tale a magical thread. Granada's palace scenes mix splendor with quiet dread.
nasa-tm-19670028225-stratospheric-temper:
Guenter Warnecke and Andrew W. McCulloch, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, presented this paper in London, England, in July 1967. The meeting was the tenth plenary session of COSPAR, the international space research committee. Their subject is temperature patterns in the stratosphere, drawn from measurements by the Nimbus II weather satellite.

The satellite's infrared radiometer imaged the Earth in a carbon dioxide absorption band that senses stratospheric temperature, alongside a clear window channel. Because clouds contaminate the picture, one section treats the elimination of cloud influence. The paper then presents stratospheric temperature distribution maps for four days in May, June, and July 1966. A typical image shows the temperature pattern running from high values over the Arctic down to low values far in the southern latitudes. The cloud pattern appears superimposed, from the window channel.
nasa-tm-19700029986-an-analytical-develo:
Richard W. Barbieri of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in August 1970. It develops, in math form, how two close satellites move in relation to each other. Both satellites circle a planet that is not a perfect sphere, but slightly flattened at the poles.

The study describes the sideways relative motion of satellites flying only a few kilometres apart. That gap is tiny beside their distance from the planet's center, which the paper takes as far larger. The work supported studies of orbiting long baseline interferometry, including the proposed Radio Astronomy Explorer pair. Equations came from a Lagrangian formulation, with the satellites' pull on each other left out.
object-lessons-on-the-human-body-a-trans:
Sarah F. Buckelew wrote Object Lessons on the Human Body from lessons given in a New York primary school. The subtitle names the primary department of School No. 49, in New York City. Parker P. Simmons issued this revised pupils' edition in 1904. It belongs to a series called Practical Work in the School Room.

Her note to the pupil calls the body the house you live in. Children must learn to guard that house from two great enemies, alcohol and nicotine. She warns them not to talk parrot fashion, saying words the mind does not grasp. Knowledge must be paid for with attention, she adds, through one's own eyes and ears. Nobody else can pay that price.
poems-vol-iv:
Hattie Howard published the fourth volume of her Poems in Hartford in 1904, from the Case, Lockwood and Brainard press. Howard was a Connecticut writer of stories and verse with titles such as Poverty versus Pauperism, Our Girls, and Keeping a Secret to her name. The volume opens with press notices of a former volume, quoted at length, praising her poems of sentiment as natural, spontaneous, direct, and free from ambitious pretense.

The reviewers stress the book's sunny, hopeful spirit, welcome in a time of morbid expression, and its hearty, wholesome human feeling, sometimes overflowing into downright fun. An illustration shows her brother Harry Howard, a student, with a motto about the pure in heart. Howard wrote for the home circle rather than the academy, and volume four, arriving after three earlier volumes, testifies to a loyal local readership for cheerful, tender, plain-spoken verse.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-louis-:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Louis XIV draws its extracts from the memoirs of the Duchesse d'Orléans. Her letters and recollections report the Sun King's court from within. Prepared by David Widger, the selection runs in alphabetical order, one pointed sentence at a time.

A pious Capuchin explains a dream, the Queen gets only the rinsings of the glass, and duplicity passes for wit while frankness counts as folly. The Duchess mocks high head-dresses, horrid swearing, and excessive bathing. She wonders aloud whether the King believes in the existence of a God at all. The volume gains its tart, gossipy flavor from such lines.
the-child-and-childhood-in-folk-thought-:
Alexander Francis Chamberlain, M.A., Ph.D., studies the child in folk thought in this book, grown from lectures he gave at Clark University's summer school in 1894. Its full title promises studies of what children do and how they shape life among early peoples, with matches and survivals in modern culture. He dedicates the work to his father and mother, with a verse from Goethe.

In his prefatory note Chamberlain ties the book to the child-study movement then drawing teachers and parents. His aim is to mark the chief things children do among primitive peoples, then trace how those acts live on in today's social forms and culture movements. The point of view, he insists, stays with the child and what the child has done in all ages and among all races. Readers get an early work of anthropology that treats children's play and custom as serious evidence.
the-tent-on-the-beach-and-other-poems-pa:
John Greenleaf Whittier's Tent on the Beach gathers narrative poems around a poetical picnic on the New Hampshire coast. His prelude names his two companions, Fields the lettered magnate and Taylor the free cosmopolite, without quite naming them. He pictures the Hampton River winding through salt-meadows near the tent. Great Boar's Head bluff stands northward, and Newburyport lifts its steeples to the south.

The contents promise legends told in the tent: The Wreck of Rivermouth, The Changeling, The Maids of Attitash, The Palatine, and Abraham Davenport. Whittier's opening verse calls his plot simple, old fancies from boyhood warmed into life again. Readers who like New England legend in ballad form will find the whole programme laid out invitingly.
the-traveling-engineers-association-to-i:
The Traveling Engineers' Association issued its examination questions and answers for firemen seeking promotion, copyrighted by W. O. Thompson in 1911 and revised in January 1919. The preface explains railroad policy: companies employ firemen who will in time become competent engineers. A candidate needs at least a common school education, good habits, sound judgment, and good physical condition. Advancement comes to men conscientious in duty who study in their leisure hours.

The question code tests how far a fireman has progressed, year by year, and guides what he must know both as fireman and as future engineer. This practical manual preserves the world of steam railroading from inside the cab. Readers meet the era's faith in self-improvement, where a workingman's promotion depended on mastering boilers, brakes, and rules through printed questions.
